title: Why Are Roads Buckling in the Heat? And Can We Fix It Before LA 2028?
summary:
Have you ever seen a road suddenly pop up and crack like a broken sidewalk? That’s called buckling, and it happened on a highway near Baltimore over the Fourth of July weekend! A heat wave baked the eastern U.S., and on Interstate 97, one lane of concrete warped so badly it had to close. Chicago had a similar problem.

So what’s going on? When roads get super hot, the pavement expands. If there’s water underneath, the ground gets squishy, and the road can crack and buckle — especially if it’s concrete. Asphalt can get soft and form ruts, like a melted chocolate bar. Scientists say climate change is making heat waves longer and hotter, and also causing heavier rain. Both can wreck roads.

Engineers know how to build tougher roads. They can add steel bars inside concrete or use special asphalt mixes that handle higher temperatures. But those upgrades cost more money. “We could design for extreme events,” says Professor Amit Bhasin from the University of Texas, “but then you have to decide: are you okay if it fails 1% of the time?”

Right now, many roads were built for milder weather. As temperatures climb, they’re reaching their breaking point. Mikhail Chester, an engineering professor at Arizona State, says we need to innovate and share new ideas. So next time you’re stuck in traffic from a buckled road, remember — it’s not just the heat, it’s a sign our roads need an upgrade for a hotter future.
why_it_matters: When roads break, it can slow down school buses, delay family trips, and cost money to fix — understanding why helps us demand safer, smarter roads for everyone.

background_read: Interstate 97 is a major highway in Maryland, near the city of Baltimore on the U.S. East Coast. Chicago is a big city in the Midwest also mentioned for similar road problems.
Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperatures and weather patterns, partly caused by burning fuels like coal and gas. It makes heat waves more common and intense.
Engineers like Amit Bhasin (a professor at the University of Texas) and Mikhail Chester (from Arizona State University) study ways to make roads survive extreme weather.
Article_Structure: WHO: Drivers, highway workers, and engineering professors like Amit Bhasin and Mikhail Chester.
WHAT: High heat caused a concrete lane to warp and buckle on Interstate 97 near Baltimore, forcing its closure; similar problems happened in Chicago.
WHERE: On a highway in Maryland (USA) and other heat-affected areas like Chicago.
WHY: Pavement expands when hot; water underneath softens the ground, and older designs were not made for today's hotter, wetter climate.

perspectives.description: Some engineers say we should spend extra money to upgrade roads with steel bars and special mixes so they last through extreme heat and heavy rain.
Others worry that making every road super-strong is too expensive and that we may have to accept that some roads will fail during rare extreme weather.
Scientists link this problem to climate change, which is making heat waves longer; this is a sign that our infrastructure needs to adapt, just like our habits to protect the planet.
